developments.title: ODS demos run local Qwen 3.8 Next Flash on RTX Spark at its official launch
detail: Ahmad reports that the official RTX Spark launch event in San Francisco drew lines of attendees waiting to try local AI demos on the device. The demos were built with ODS and ran a local Qwen 3.8 Next Flash model rather than cloud inference.
He adds that local AI is becoming capable on hardware that does not require a basement setup or 240V breakers.
developments.why_it_matters: A complete local model stack — ODS software serving Qwen 3.8 Next Flash — ran directly on the RTX Spark at its launch, letting attendees try capable local inference on hardware without a dedicated high-power setup.

developments.title: maya-ik2 runs Inkling 2 Mini at 128 tok/s with 344K context on one RTX 3090
detail: Alexey Fateev reports that his maya-ik2 engine runs Inkling 2 Mini on a single RTX 3090 at 128.7 tok/s decode, or 129.5 tok/s over HTTP, with a 344K context. The GitHub listing corroborates the project's headline 128 tok/s and 344K-context results; his measurements show 124.2 tok/s at 4K context and 62.3 tok/s at 340K, versus 57.0 tok/s from llama.cpp for short prompts. The engine keeps all 3,072 experts resident in VRAM, consolidates 7,350 kernel launches into 781 within one CUDA graph, and uses custom FP8 KV-attention and NVFP4 expert kernels. On the RTX 3090, the expert kernel unpacks 4-bit weights into FP16 registers for Tensor Core processing; Fateev also moved BF16 vision processing to CPU, added a thinking-off toggle, and reports GSM8K scores of 74/96 versus 73/96 for the scalar path, with a 5.7e-5 KL difference.
developments.why_it_matters: Users can now use the published configuration as a baseline when choosing between llama.cpp and a CUDA-graph, expert-resident engine for long-context local inference.

external_links.title: GitHub - alesha-pro/maya-inkling-mini: Inkling 2 Mini on one RTX 3090: 128 tok/s, 344K context, images and tools. A Project Maya engine (maya-ik2) with every expert in VRAM. · GitHub

developments.title: Alexey Fateev open-sources a playbook for optimizing 400B+ MoE models on 4x RTX 3090s
detail: Alexey Fateev released a playbook based on optimizing 400B+ MoE models on four RTX 3090s, with a workflow and skill usable in Claude Code or Codex. It catalogs 102 tested hypotheses across six models and 16 chapters, including 40 failures and exact hardware conditions.

Reported results include a 3.6x speedup for cold CPU experts after disabling PDEP and a DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 32K prefill increase from 430 to 2,199 tokens/sec after rewriting DMA and chunked loading. Reported negative or mixed results include prompt-selected experts covering only 48% of answer experts on Hy4 Flash, a static hot-expert profile reaching 64-69% versus 61% random placement on MiniMax-M3.1-Flash in simulation, and a Cyrillic draft vocabulary raising Qwen3.8-Flash-Next acceptance from 32% to 54%.
Each entry includes hardware tags, raw measurements, failure details, and retesting guidance. The repository is intended for reuse by users and coding agents.
developments.why_it_matters: Engineers running large MoE models on consumer GPUs can use hardware-tagged pass and fail results to decide which optimizations are worth retesting on their setup.

external_links.title: GitHub - alesha-pro/inference-optimization-playbook: 97 tested hypotheses on making huge MoE LLMs fast on consumer GPUs (4x RTX 3090 + experts in RAM): what worked, what failed and why. A playbook for people and a ready skill for coding agents. · GitHub

developments.title: Maziyar Panahi trains a robot arm to rack specimen vials
detail: Maziyar Panahi reports a robot arm learning to rack specimen vials across 4,096 simulated benches, reaching 1,010 successful racks out of 1,024 attempts after about 27 minutes on one GPU. Progress was zero at iteration 200, then 24 at 250 and 843 at 300.
developments.why_it_matters: Lab automation engineers can use this run as a reference point for reinforcement-learning pick-and-place training on a single GPU.

developments.title: M3 Ultra Mac Studio cluster runs GLM‑5.3 8‑bit model
detail: A user reported optimizing GLM‑5.3 8‑bit inference on Apple M3 Ultra Mac Studio hardware.
The same poster notes they are operating four such machines together as a cluster.
This shows that high‑throughput local inference of the GLM‑5.3 model is feasible on Apple silicon.
developments.why_it_matters: You can now run GLM‑5.3 locally on affordable Mac hardware, enabling private inference without cloud services.

developments.title: Lean and Mathlib certify Levent Alpöge's Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis
detail: Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library of 17 million lines on November 20. The Lean and Mathlib communities subsequently verified it and issued a joint statement certifying it as correct.
The proof comprises 175,000 modules and compiled with three standard axioms; independent checkers cleared a 61.6 GB proof export. The 17-million-line library is described as Claude-written Lean.
Lean FRO's statement says it looks forward to mathematical community activity that will explain the new ideas in the proof.
developments.why_it_matters: Researchers can now build on or audit a machine-checked proof rather than an unchecked 940-page human draft.

developments.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen's 'xhigh' thinking effort draws roughly 6x the tokens and cost of 'high' in Simon Willison's pelican comparison
detail: Simon Willison reports a very significant gap between Gemini 4 Hydrogen running at 'high' versus 'xhigh' thinking effort, sharing side-by-side pelican outputs for the two settings. The 'high' run used 5,311 output tokens and cost 3.99 cents, while the identical model at 'xhigh' used 31,477 output tokens and cost 23.61 cents. That is roughly a sixfold increase in both output tokens and dollar cost driven only by the effort setting.
developments.why_it_matters: For the exact same model, moving the thinking-effort dial from 'high' to 'xhigh' multiplied output token count and cost by about six times. Thinking-effort selection is therefore a direct, immediate cost lever when running Gemini 4 Hydrogen.

developments.title: DeepSeek Flash and GLM 5.3 priced 60% lower than Fireworks and Baseten
detail: The provider announced that DeepSeek Flash and GLM 5.3 are being sold at a price 60% lower than competing offerings from Fireworks and Baseten.
A quoted OpenCode post confirms that both models are currently listed at a 60% discount.
The announcement also claims the service now handles more inference volume than the competitors, though that aspect lacks independent verification.
developments.why_it_matters: The steep price reduction makes high‑performance large language models more accessible to cost‑sensitive users, potentially shifting demand away from existing commercial providers.

developments.title: Tesla FSD v15 adds Reality View, a live visualization of FSD's planned driving actions
detail: A quoted post says Tesla FSD v15 adds "Reality View," described as a live visualization of the drive.
According to that post, the feature lets users see and control what FSD is planning to do.
developments.why_it_matters: The feature gives drivers visibility into FSD's planned actions and an ability to control those plans during a drive.

developments.title: Hex dictation app launches on iOS App Store
detail: Hex, a fully local fast dictation tool, has been released on the iOS App Store.
The app offers 100% free usage and performs speech‑to‑text processing entirely on‑device, eliminating the need for cloud services.
developments.why_it_matters: Users can now perform offline, privacy‑preserving dictation on iOS devices without paying for a subscription.

developments.title: ChatGPT/Codex Desktop App Update Adds Space for Plus and Performance Boosts
detail: The latest desktop app release introduces ChatGPT Space for Plus, a redesigned visual layout, and rebuilt thread handling for faster performance. Additional enhancements include a refreshed Space home, quicker page and slide rendering, mobile page editing, and a more reliable Codex Remote connection.
developments.why_it_matters: You can now edit pages on mobile, enabling on‑the‑go content creation without relying on cloud services.

developments.title: macOS version of cc-switcher targets purpose-isolated subscriptions
detail: Greg Pstrucha created a macOS version of cc-switcher for workflows where subscriptions are kept purpose-isolated.
The implementation is intended for cases where CLIProxy is unnecessary, and users can point their agent at the repository to request setup.
It adapts the existing project to macOS rather than introducing a broader cross-platform rewrite.
developments.why_it_matters: Mac users with separate agent subscriptions can switch contexts without adopting CLIProxy.

developments.title: Quinn Slack trains a local "Hey Puck" wake-word model with Amp-generated data
detail: Quinn Slack reports training a local wake-word model that triggers on "Hey Puck," with the Amp coding agent generating the synthetic training data. The model was trained on 77.2 hours of Slack's own dictation recordings, with no training on other people's data.
Amp also helped gather recordings from additional microphones and built native Swift, Kotlin, and Web implementations of the wake word.
developments.why_it_matters: Developers can hand a coding agent their own recordings and get a private cross-platform wake word without collecting any third-party training data.

developments.title: Vercel Labs deepsec uses glm‑flash for continuous local security scanning
detail: Vercel Labs’ deepsec tool is being run continuously with the local glm‑flash model to scan for security issues.
The setup has identified hundreds of vulnerabilities over a week, which are then handed off to an agent council using Theo’s tstack skill for remediation.
developments.why_it_matters: You can now run nonstop AI‑driven vulnerability detection locally, reducing reliance on cloud services and catching issues faster.
